To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the error ellipse for the position of a binary black hole on the sky evolves rapidly over a few days prior to coalescence, (2) the error ellipse can be localized to ~ 10 deg2 a month prior to coalesence, and (3) the error in the distance can be determined to a few percent.

GWs can locate a massive black hole binary coalecsence to within a few tens of deg2 and determine the source's distance to several percent, with the accuracy of the localization and distance determination degrading slowly as the merger approaches.

GWs will be able to localize a coalescence of massive black holes to within a few tens of square degrees, and determine distance and redshift to several percent accuracy, as soon as a month before merger, and that this localization will be dominated by weak lensing.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the localization and redshift determination of massive black hole binary (MBHB) coalescences by gravitational wave (GWs) observatories, and in particular, with the evolution of the GW error ellipses as a function of time.
the detection and localization of massive black hole binary mergers with the LISA mission.
the localization of massive black hole binary coalecences with gravitational waves.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
LISA would be able to localize a coalescence within 10 deg2 and determine its luminosity distance (and redshift) to a few percent.

GW observations alone can localize a coalescence of massive black hole binaries to a region of a few square degrees, which is small enough for optical follow-up, and determine the distance (and hence the redshift) to a percent level.
the GW localization of massive BH binaries will be very useful to help identify the host galaxies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the GW localizability will improve by a factor of 3-10 over 10 years prior to merger.
the GW localization error ellipse will shrink in size with time and the GW distance error will shrink with time, but both will increase with source distance.
the localization of coalescing massive black hole binaries is very good.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the GWs can localize a coalescence to a region of the sky small enough that it is worth searching for the host galaxies of the event.
GWs can provide a good initial localization of a coalescence even before the source is in its final stages of inspiral.
GWs can localize binaries to an area of a few square degrees, which will be useful for identifying the host galaxies of massive black hole binary mergers.
